subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: What Is Data? Recognising and Categorising Information

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates? (Open-ended process question on data organisation.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the most popular game in their class? (Read and interpret the raw data list to identify hockey as the most frequent.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pari wants to respond to four questions. Put a tick for questions requiring data collection and a cross for those that do not: (a) most popular TV show among classmates; (b) when India got independence; (c) water wasted in her locality; (d) capital of India.

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: "What is data?" Students brainstorm examples from daily life — heights of classmates, favourite colours, temperatures. Establish that data is any collection of facts, numbers, measures, observations, or descriptions that convey information, drawing directly from the section's definition.

Students examine a raw, unorganised list of favourite games. Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.75 ("What would you do to find the most popular game among Naresh's and Navya's classmates?") is posed for pair discussion. Students then answer Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.75 ("What is the most popular game in their class?") by scanning the unorganised list, experiencing how difficult it is without structure.

Introduce tally marks as a systematic tool. Students recreate the frequency table for the games data using tally marks, counting each category carefully. Whole-class check: confirm the frequency of each game and confirm which is most popular, reinforcing the definition of frequency.

Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.75 ("Pari wants to respond to four questions…") is presented. Students individually decide which questions need data collection and which do not, then share reasoning. Close by restating: some questions are answered by existing facts; others require fresh collection.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating any list of numbers as data — students benefit from the clarification that data must convey information about something real. Watch for students who mark the capital of India as needing collection; prompt them to distinguish a fixed, recorded fact from a question whose answer varies by context or person. For self-study, Example, section 4.2 p.80 shows a worked pictograph that extends the idea of organising data visually.

periods.activity_title: Tally Tables, Shoe Sizes, and Real Data Tasks

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet-preference data. Sub-parts: (a) students who chose jalebi; (b) barfi count; (c) gujiya count; (d) rasgulla count; (e) gulab jamun count.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student? Explain. If not, what is the alternative?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order: (a) largest shoe size; (b) smallest shoe size; (c) number of students wearing size 5; (d) number wearing sizes larger than 4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: How did arranging the data in ascending order help answer the shoe-size questions?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78
homework.description: Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school, record observations, complete a frequency table, then answer: (a) tree found in greatest number; (b) tree in smallest number; (c) any two trees found in equal numbers.

time_bands.activity: Students open with Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.76 ("Complete the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet-preference data…"). Working individually, they fill all five sub-parts, applying tally marks to a new dataset. Pairs compare tallies and resolve any discrepancies.

Whole-class discussion of Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 ("Is the frequency table sufficient to distribute each type of sweet to the correct student?…"). Students reason that a frequency table shows how many of each type but not who chose what, and suggest an alternative such as a name-keyed list. This surfaces the distinction between aggregate (frequency) and individual records.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 4.1 p.77 ("Help Sushri Sandhya figure out from shoe-size data arranged in ascending order…"), reading the ordered dataset to answer all four sub-parts. They then address Figure it Out Q2, section 4.1 p.77 ("How did arranging the data in ascending order help?") in a brief Math Talk, articulating the benefit of ordering.

Introduce Figure it Out Q4, section 4.1 p.78 ("Write names of trees seen on the way from home to school…") as a take-home task. Walk through what a complete frequency table for this task looks like: students list categories first, then tally on their own route. Clarify that the route and trees will differ for each student — that variety is the point.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse ascending order with the frequency count — watch for those who sort by frequency instead of sorting the raw data values themselves. The shoe-size exercise is an ideal moment to reinforce that the same data can answer different questions depending on how it is arranged. Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.77 ("Are there other ways to arrange the shoe-size data?") offers a rich discussion extension for fast finishers.
materials: Blank frequency table template on board

periods.activity_title: Collecting Data from Newspapers and Real Surveys

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.75
textbook_items_in_class.description: Try to find out the most popular game among your own classmates. (Real data collection activity.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x and one other of your choice, fill a frequency table. Sub-parts: (a) most frequent letter; (b) least frequent letter; (c) list the five letters in ascending frequency order and compare with classmates; (d) write the process followed; (e) discuss classmates' processes; (f) what process would you follow with a different article?

time_bands.activity: Launch Figure it Out Q3, section 4.1 p.75 ("Try to find out the most popular game among your own classmates…"). Students quickly survey their immediate neighbours, recording responses as a raw list, then transfer to a tally-frequency table. Groups of four share and reconcile their tables.

Students turn to Figure it Out Q5, section 4.1 p.78 ("Paste a newspaper article, count letters c, e, i, r, x and one other of your choice…"). Using a short printed passage provided by the teacher, students tally all six letters and complete the frequency table, then answer sub-parts (a)–(c): most frequent, least frequent, and ascending-order list.

Pairs compare their ascending-order lists from the letter-frequency table. Students then work on sub-parts (d)–(f): writing their process, discussing a classmate's approach, and explaining how the process would change for a different article. This surfaces that method, not just result, is part of data handling.

Brief whole-class share: one or two students describe their process in their own words. Consolidate by naming the full cycle explored across this section: collect raw data → organise with tally marks → read the frequency table to answer questions.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes tally letters by scanning randomly and double-counting; encourage a single left-to-right pass with a finger. Watch for ascending-order errors where students list by letter name rather than by frequency — the ordering criterion here is frequency, not alphabetical sequence. For self-study, Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98 offers a full bar-graph construction task that builds directly on the kind of frequency table students are building here.
materials: Short printed text passage (one per student or pair)

periods.activity_title: Pictographs: Reading Symbols and Understanding Scale

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.2 p.80
textbook_items_in_class.description: Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours. Students read the pictograph (each symbol = 10 children) to find: children who always slept ≥9 hours (50), sometimes (25), and never (40). Full solutions provided demonstrating how to handle full and half symbols.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk: What problems would arise in preparing a pictograph (where one symbol = 10 students, half = 5) if the total number of students in a class is 33 or 27?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Middle School Ginnori library over a week to answer: (a) day with minimum books borrowed; (b) total books borrowed during the week; (c) day with maximum books borrowed and possible reason.

time_bands.activity: Establish the definition of a pictograph: data represented through pictures or symbols, each carrying a stated key that gives the symbol's value. Ask students what they already recall about pictographs from earlier classes, briefly gathering responses without evaluating. Introduce the term 'scale' or 'key' as the stated number of units one symbol represents.

Walk through Example, section 4.2 p.80 ("Nand Kishor's pictograph on how often middle-school children slept at least 9 hours…"). Students read along: each full symbol equals 10 children; a half symbol equals 5. Identify the 'Always', 'Sometimes', 'Never' rows, compute counts, and confirm the given answers. Highlight how a half-symbol arises when a value is not a multiple of the key.

Students answer Figure it Out Q1, section 4.2 p.83 ("Use the pictograph of books borrowed from Middle School Ginnori library over a week…") individually, then compare with a partner. Focus attention on reading the key first before counting symbols.

Math Talk, section 4.2 p.83 ("What problems would arise… if the total number of students is 33 or 27?"): students reason in pairs about why 33 and 27 are problematic when the key is 10 (with halves representing 5). Collect two or three responses; establish that values not expressible as multiples of the key unit or its half create ambiguity or fractions of symbols.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently read symbols without consulting the key, leading to answers that are off by the scale factor. Insist that checking the key is the first step every time. A half-symbol causing confusion is especially common — use Nand Kishor's 'Sometimes' row (25 children = 2 full + 1 half) as the reference example whenever this arises. For self-study, Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84 has students construct a pictograph with half-symbols, extending what they have read here.
materials: Coloured chalk or markers to illustrate symbols

periods.activity_title: Drawing Pictographs and Choosing a Scale

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84
textbook_items_in_class.description: Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai's kite sales data (Chaman 250, Rani 300, Rukhsana 100, Jasmeet 450, Jetha Lal 250, Poonam Ben 700). Answer: (a) symbols for Rani; (b) maximum buyer; (c) Jasmeet vs Chaman; (d) whether Poonam Ben bought more than double Rani's amount.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the structural features of a pictograph established via Nand Kishor's sleep-habits example: data arranged in rows or columns, each row labelled, a key stating the symbol's value, half-symbols for intermediate values. Pose the question: what happens when data values are in the hundreds? Introduce the idea that a larger key reduces the number of symbols needed.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.2 p.84 ("Prepare a pictograph using one symbol = 100 kites for Magan Bhai's kite sales data…"). They draw the pictograph in their notebooks, handling half-symbols where needed (e.g., Chaman = 2.5 symbols, Jetha Lal = 2.5 symbols). After construction, they answer sub-parts (a)–(d) using their own completed graph.

Pairs exchange notebooks and verify each other's pictograph and answers. Teacher leads a quick check: confirm Poonam Ben's row (7 symbols) and Rukhsana's row (1 symbol), then address sub-part (d) by comparing 700 with double of 300 (600) — yes, Poonam Ben bought more than double. Discuss any cases where a half-symbol was placed incorrectly.

Summarise the key properties recalled from the section: pictographs give a visual impression, support quick comparison, require a clearly stated key, and become difficult when values are large or not exact multiples of the chosen key unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error here is omitting the key or drawing it without stating the unit value. Watch also for students who draw 2.5 symbols as two full symbols (rounding down) — reinforce that a half-symbol is the accepted representation for half the key unit. For self-study, Example, section 4.3 p.87 introduces bar graphs as a more precise alternative and is worth reading after completing this pictograph construction.
materials: Pencil and plain or squared paper

periods.activity_title: Bar Graphs: Structure, Scale, and Reading

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the bar graph of students absent per class (Classes I–VIII) to answer: In Class 2, how many were absent? Which class had maximum absences? Which class had full attendance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.3 p.87
textbook_items_in_class.description: Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a busy Delhi road crossing from 6 am to 12 noon (one unit = 100 vehicles). Demonstrates reading maximum (7–8 am, 1200 vehicles), minimum (6–7 am, ~150 vehicles), second highest, and computing combined intervals (8–10 am total ~1800 vehicles).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many total vehicles passed through the Delhi crossing between 6 am and noon?

time_bands.activity: Introduce bar graphs as a more precise alternative to pictographs: bars of uniform width, equal spacing, a scale on one axis, and length or height encoding frequency. Identify the two axes — categories on one, frequency scale on the other — and state the rule that the scale axis must start from zero. Draw a minimal labelled sketch on the board.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.86 ("Use the bar graph of students absent per class, Classes I–VIII…"), reading the vertical bar graph to answer the three sub-parts. Confirm answers whole-class, paying attention to any bar that reaches zero (full attendance) and the bar that reaches the highest point.

Walk through Example, section 4.3 p.87 ("Horizontal bar graph of vehicular traffic at a busy Delhi road crossing…"). Students follow along, identifying the key (one unit = 100 vehicles), locating the maximum and minimum bars, and computing the 8–10 am combined total. Emphasise that a horizontal bar graph uses the same structural rules; only the orientation differs.

Students answer Figure it Out Q1, section 4.3 p.88 ("How many total vehicles passed through the Delhi crossing between 6 am and noon?") independently. A brief share confirms the total, and the teacher notes that adding bar heights is straightforward once the scale is read correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often misread horizontal bar graphs because they instinctively look at vertical height; remind them that in a horizontal bar graph the bar's length to the right encodes the frequency, not its vertical position. A common arithmetic slip is reading the scale incorrectly — for instance reading a bar ending halfway between two gridlines as the lower value. Use the Delhi traffic example's 6–7 am bar (~150 vehicles) to illustrate careful reading between gridlines. For self-study, Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.89 ("India population bar graph, Math Talk") extends the reading task to larger numbers.
materials: Chalkboard sketch of a labelled bar graph

periods.activity_title: Reasoning from Bar Graphs: Traffic Patterns and Population

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think so little traffic occurred during 6–7 am compared to later hours?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think traffic was heaviest between 7–8 am?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.3 p.88
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why do you think traffic was lesser and lesser each hour after 8 am until noon?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.89
textbook_items_in_class.description: Math Talk on India population bar graph: (a) what questions might you ask friends based on the graph; (b) how much did population increase over 50 years and in each decade?

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the Delhi vehicular traffic bar graph read in the previous unit, recalling the key structural features: bars of uniform width, a scale starting from zero, and frequency encoded in bar length. Frame today's focus: using a bar graph not just to read values but to reason about the story behind the data.

Students work through Figure it Out Q2, Q3, and Q4, section 4.3 p.88 ("Why so little traffic at 6–7 am?", "Why heaviest at 7–8 am?", "Why decreasing after 8 am?") in small groups. Each group writes a brief justification for each question drawing on real-world knowledge. Groups share reasoning; teacher notes that bar graphs invite contextual interpretation, not just numerical reading.

Students examine the India population bar graph (vertical bars, one unit = 10 crores) in Figure it Out, section 4.3 p.89. They generate their own questions for sub-part (a), then compute total population increase over 50 years and decade-by-decade increases for sub-part (b), writing calculations beside the graph.

Whole-class share of one or two student-generated questions from the population graph. Close by summarising: bar graphs allow fast identification of the largest and smallest categories and enable computation of totals and differences, making them more precise than pictographs for large or varied datasets.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may give vague answers ("more people travel at 7–8 am") without connecting to the data; prompt them to frame their reasoning as "the bar for 7–8 am is the tallest, suggesting…". A common error in the population graph task is computing the increase over 50 years as the sum of all bars rather than as the difference between the last and first bars; address this during the whole-class share. For self-study, Example, section 4.4 p.90 shows how a scale is chosen when values are large, extending what students practised here.
materials: Pencil and paper for written justifications

periods.activity_title: Step-by-Step Bar Graph Construction: Scale and Axes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.4 p.90
textbook_items_in_class.description: Vertical bar graph of runs scored by Smriti in 8 cricket matches (scores: 80, 50, 10, 100, 90, 0, 90, 50). Demonstrates selecting scale of 1 unit = 10 runs to avoid impractically tall bars and drawing the completed bar graph.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 4.4 p.91
textbook_items_in_class.description: Vertical bar graph of Imran's family monthly expenditure across six items (house rent ₹3000, food ₹3400, education ₹800, electricity ₹400, transport ₹600, miscellaneous ₹1200). Demonstrates scale selection (1 unit = ₹200), computing bar heights by division (e.g. house rent = 15 units), and drawing and reading the completed bar graph.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use Imran's expenditure bar graph to answer: (1) which item family spends most and second most on; (2) is electricity cost about half the education cost; (3) is education cost less than one-fourth the food cost?

time_bands.activity: State the five-step procedure for drawing a bar graph: (1) draw two perpendicular axes; (2) label categories on the horizontal axis; (3) choose an appropriate scale; (4) compute bar heights by dividing each frequency by the scale unit; (5) draw bars of uniform width with equal spacing. Write these steps on the board and keep them visible throughout.

Walk through Example, section 4.4 p.90 ("Vertical bar graph of runs scored by Smriti in 8 cricket matches…"). Show why a scale of 1 unit = 10 runs is chosen: the maximum value is 100, requiring only 10 units on the axis — a manageable height. Students copy the completed bar graph and label axes.

Walk through Example, section 4.4 p.91 ("Vertical bar graph of Imran's family monthly expenditure…"). Demonstrate scale selection (1 unit = ₹200) and compute bar heights for each item by division: house rent = 3000 ÷ 200 = 15 units. Students draw the full bar graph in their notebooks, labelling both axes and stating the scale.

Students answer Figure it Out, section 4.4 p.93 ("Use Imran's expenditure bar graph to answer…") using their completed graph, checking sub-parts (2) and (3) by comparing bar heights numerically. Brief oral confirmation of answers closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error is choosing a scale that produces fractional bar heights — for instance using 1 unit = ₹300 for Imran's data where electricity (₹400) becomes 1.33 units, undrawn. Reinforce that the scale must be chosen so every data value divides evenly (or nearly so) into the unit. Also watch for students who draw bars of unequal width; stress that uniform width is a structural rule, not an aesthetic preference. For self-study, Example, section 4.4 p.90 (Smriti's cricket graph) can be reviewed again to consolidate scale-selection reasoning.

periods.activity_title: Bar Graph Practice: Insects, Railways, Transport and More

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden: Mites 6, Caterpillars 10, Beetles 5, Butterflies 3, Grasshoppers 2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pooja's partially erased bar graph of railway tickets sold for five MP cities (Vidisha 24, Jabalpur 20, Seoni 16, Indore 28, Sagar 16). Sub-parts: (a) tickets for Vidisha; (b) for Jabalpur; (c) determine the scale; (d) draw correct bar for Sagar; (e) add scale numbers to vertical axis; (f) are Seoni and Indore bars correct?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shagufta and Divya's bar graph of tiger counts in India 2006–2022 (in 4-year intervals: 1400, 1700, 2200, 3000, 3700) contains mistakes. Identify and fix the errors in the bars.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98
homework.description: Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities (Playing 45, Reading 30, Watching TV 20, Listening to music 10, Painting 15). Draw a bar graph (1 unit = 5 students). Which activity is preferred most after playing?

time_bands.activity: Students work independently on Figure it Out Q1, section 4.4 p.93 ("Help Samantha prepare a bar graph for insects seen in a tea garden…"), choosing a scale (1 unit = 1 insect is natural here given the small values), drawing axes, labelling categories, computing heights, and drawing all five bars. Pairs check each other's scale labelling and bar heights.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 4.4 p.93 ("Pooja's partially erased bar graph of railway tickets…"), a diagnostic task requiring them to determine the scale from what remains visible, read the existing bars, draw the missing Sagar bar, and assess whether the Seoni and Indore bars are correctly drawn. This demands both scale-determination and error-detection skills.

Students examine Figure it Out Q11, section 4.4 p.99 ("Shagufta and Divya's bar graph of tiger counts in India 2006–2022 contains mistakes…"). They identify errors in the bars — incorrect heights, unequal widths, or incorrect spacing — and redraw the corrected version. Teacher circulates, asking students to name the specific rule each error violates.

Assign Figure it Out Q9, section 4.4 p.98 ("Survey of 120 students' preferred free-time activities…") as a take-home task. Confirm the scale (1 unit = 5 students) and verify that all values divide evenly, so no fractional heights arise.

periods.teacher_notes: Figure it Out Q2 (railway tickets) is particularly valuable because students must infer the scale from the partially visible graph before they can answer anything — watch for those who assume a scale of 1 unit = 1 ticket and then find bar heights inconsistent with the visible bars. For Q11 (tiger counts), common errors include bars that do not start from zero and unequal time intervals being represented as equal widths; both are good discussion points about what makes a bar graph honest and accurate.

periods.activity_title: Extended Practice: Dice Experiments, Tractors, and Cricket

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare frequency distribution table with tally marks. Find: (a) number appearing minimum times; (b) number appearing maximum times; (c) numbers appearing equal number of times.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95
textbook_items_in_class.description: Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches. Sub-parts: (a) what information does the table give; (b) possible title; (c) what catches attention; (d) matches with 4 wickets; (e) why Mayank's method of adding 0+1+2+...+7 is wrong; (f) correct method to find total wickets.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 4.4 p.96
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tractors pictograph for five villages. Answer: (a) village with fewest tractors; (b) most tractors; (c) how many more tractors Village C has than Village B; (d) is Komal correct that Village D has half the tractors of Village E?

time_bands.activity: Students carry out Figure it Out Q4, section 4.4 p.95 ("Roll a die 30 times, record outcomes, prepare a frequency distribution table with tally marks…"). Working in pairs, one student rolls and calls, the other tallies. After 30 rolls, students complete the frequency table and answer sub-parts (a)–(c). Pairs compare results with another pair and note whether the same number was most frequent.

Students work through Figure it Out Q5, section 4.4 p.95 ("Faiz's frequency table of Bumrah's wickets in 30 matches…"), focusing especially on sub-parts (e) and (f): why Mayank's method of summing 0 through 7 is wrong (it ignores how many times each wicket count occurred) and the correct method of multiplying each wicket count by its frequency before summing.

Students answer Figure it Out Q6, section 4.4 p.96 ("Tractors pictograph for five villages…"), reading the pictograph and performing the comparisons in sub-parts (a)–(d), including verifying Komal's claim. This revisits pictograph-reading skills in a new context and reinforces comparison reasoning.

Brief whole-class discussion: what can a frequency table tell you that a raw list cannot? Consolidate the idea that frequency tables (whether for games, runs, dice or wickets) compress information in a way that supports quick comparison and calculation.

periods.teacher_notes: In the dice activity, students sometimes stop tallying after reaching a round number for one face rather than completing all 30 rolls — insist that 30 rolls is the full experiment. For the Bumrah wickets question, Mayank's error (adding 0+1+2+…+7 = 28 instead of weighting by frequency) is a conceptual misunderstanding about frequency tables, not an arithmetic slip — address it as such. The pictograph in Q6 is a good moment to contrast the precision limits of pictographs with the bar graphs students have been constructing.
materials: One die per pair of students
Tally sheet or blank notebook page

periods.activity_title: Design or Distort? Reasoning About Visual Data Choices

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: Would you use vertical or horizontal bars to represent heights of the tallest persons in each class in your school? Why?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103
textbook_items_in_class.description: For a table of longest rivers on each continent, would you prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why? Find the data, make the table and bar graph. Which continents have the longest rivers?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the principle governing this section: scale selection and bar orientation both affect how naturally a graph communicates its data, and artistic choices can mislead readers if they imply information not present in the data. Present the mountain-heights example from section 4.5: vertical bars feel more intuitive for height; horizontal bars suit lengths running parallel to the ground.

Students answer Figure it Out Q1, section 4.5 p.103 ("Would you use vertical or horizontal bars to represent heights of the tallest persons in each class in your school? Why?") in writing. Discuss two or three responses: the key reasoning is that height is a vertical dimension and vertical bars mirror that physical reality, making the graph more intuitive.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 4.5 p.103 ("For a table of longest rivers on each continent, would you prefer vertical or horizontal bars? Why? Find the data, make the table and bar graph."). Students discuss orientation choice (horizontal bars suit river lengths running across land), compile data for the six inhabited continents, choose a scale, and draw the bar graph in their notebooks.

Introduce infographics: visually enriched data presentations using imagery. Describe the caution raised in section 4.5 — using triangles of varying widths for mountains implies that taller mountains are also wider, which can mislead. Students articulate in one sentence why visual appeal must not compromise accuracy, and suggest one way to make a mountain infographic honest (e.g., equal-width triangles, or use plain bars with a mountain image as a background only).

periods.teacher_notes: Students often default to vertical bars regardless of the data type; the bar-orientation question is designed to make them reason about what the data represents physically, not just apply a default. Watch for reasoning that conflates aesthetic preference ("vertical looks nicer") with principled choice; prompt students to connect the orientation to what the measured quantity is. The infographics caution — that artistic choices can mislead — is central to the section's closing argument and worth dwelling on: ask students whether they have ever seen an infographic that made a comparison look larger or smaller than the numbers suggest.
materials: Reference data for longest rivers (textbook or provided sheet)

items.prompt: Which of the following BEST describes what a tally mark is used for when organising raw data?

options.label: A
options.text: To arrange all data values from smallest to largest

options.label: B
options.text: To calculate the total number of items by multiplying categories

options.label: C
options.text: To count and record how many times each category appears in a raw list

options.label: D
options.text: To draw a picture that represents each item of data

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Tally marks are used to count and record how many times each category appears in a raw list, producing the frequency of each category.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition of tally marks as a counting and recording tool for building a frequency table from raw data.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing tally marks with pictograph symbols; both organise data but through different means.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is conflating tally-mark organisation with ascending-order arrangement, a separate step in data handling.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has a procedural misconception, thinking frequency involves multiplication rather than counting.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the tally-marks frequency table for Shri Nilesh's sweet data in their textbook.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one more real-life example where tally marks would be useful and explain why.

items.prompt: In a pictograph, the key states that one symbol represents 10 children. A row shows 3 full symbols and one half symbol. How many children does that row represent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — 3 full symbols = 3 × 10 = 30 children; 1 half symbol = 5 children; total = 35 children.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of full symbols by the key value and add half the key value for each half symbol.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted only the full symbols and ignored the half symbol entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student counted the half symbol as a full symbol, adding 10 instead of 5.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted only the half symbol's contribution (5) times something, possibly misreading the row.

inclusivity.support: Let the student revisit the Nand Kishor sleep-habits worked example where half symbols are explicitly explained.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words what a row of 2 full symbols and 1 half symbol represents when the key is 1 symbol = 4 children.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a structural rule that EVERY bar graph must follow?

options.label: A
options.text: Bars must always be drawn vertically, never horizontally

options.label: B
options.text: Each bar must be a different colour to distinguish categories

options.label: C
options.text: The frequency axis must start from zero and each bar must have the same width

options.label: D
options.text: The number of bars must be fewer than five

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The frequency (scale) axis must start from zero, and all bars must be of uniform width; these are the defining structural rules of a bar graph.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the structural properties of bar graphs stated in section 4.3: uniform bar width, equal spacing, and scale starting from zero.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not grasped that bar orientation (vertical or horizontal) is a design choice, not a fixed rule.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is confusing a typical example with a rule; there is no limit on the number of bars.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing a common visual convention with a structural requirement.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the absent-students bar graph in the textbook and identify the scale axis starting point.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name one more property of a well-drawn bar graph and explain what goes wrong if it is violated.

items.prompt: A student wants to display the depths of the deepest lakes on each continent in a bar graph. She asks: should I use vertical bars or horizontal bars? Explain which orientation is more appropriate and why, using the reasoning about physical intuition from this chapter.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Horizontal bars are more appropriate. Depth goes downward, which is a vertical direction, but bar graphs representing a quantity that extends below a surface are more intuitively read as horizontal bars running across the page — matching the visual image of looking at a lake from the side. Alternatively, one could argue vertical bars pointing downward would mirror depth literally; either orientation is acceptable if the student provides a principled physical reason. The key is that orientation should be chosen to match the physical nature of the quantity, not selected arbitrarily.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the section 4.5 principle that bar orientation should match the physical intuition of the quantity being represented (height uses vertical bars; length along the ground uses horizontal bars).

inclusivity.support: Think aloud with a partner about whether depth goes side to side or up and down, then connect that direction to a bar's orientation.
inclusivity.challenge: What if the data were depths of ocean trenches instead of lakes — would you change your answer? Explain any difference.

items.prompt: A teacher asks 20 students to name their favourite fruit. The raw responses are: Mango, Apple, Banana, Mango, Guava, Apple, Mango, Banana, Apple, Mango, Guava, Mango, Apple, Banana, Mango, Apple, Guava, Mango, Banana, Apple. Organise this data into a tally-marks frequency table. Then answer: (a) Which fruit is most popular? (b) How many more students chose Mango than Guava? (c) List the four fruits in ascending order of frequency.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Tally and frequency table: Mango — 7, Apple — 6, Banana — 4, Guava — 3. Total = 20. (a) Mango is the most popular fruit. (b) 7 − 3 = 4 more students chose Mango than Guava. (c) Ascending order of frequency: Guava (3), Banana (4), Apple (6), Mango (7).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Tally each fruit from the raw list, compute frequencies, then read off the maximum, compute a difference, and order by frequency.

inclusivity.support: Draw a blank three-column table (Fruit | Tally | Frequency) and go through the list one item at a time, making a mark under each fruit's tally column.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one Guava to Banana — how does the frequency table and the ascending order change? Re-solve with the new data.

items.prompt: The letters in a short passage are counted and recorded. The frequency table shows: A — 12, E — 18, I — 9, O — 15, U — 6. (a) List the five vowels in ascending order of frequency. (b) What is the difference in frequency between the most frequent and least frequent vowels? (c) What fraction of the total vowel count does E represent? (Express as a simplified fraction.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Ascending order: U (6), I (9), A (12), O (15), E (18). (b) Difference = 18 − 6 = 12. (c) Total = 12 + 18 + 9 + 15 + 6 = 60; E's fraction = 18/60 = 3/10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read frequencies from the table, sort by frequency for ascending order, subtract for the difference, and simplify the ratio of E's frequency to the total.

inclusivity.support: Write the five frequencies on separate slips and physically arrange them from smallest to largest before answering part (a).
inclusivity.challenge: If two more E's and one fewer U were found, how would the fraction for E change? Re-compute and compare.

items.prompt: A village survey records the number of bicycles owned in five streets: Street 1 — 30, Street 2 — 50, Street 3 — 20, Street 4 — 40, Street 5 — 35. A student decides to use a pictograph with a key of 1 symbol = 10 bicycles. (a) How many symbols (including any half-symbols) will each street require? (b) Which street will have the most symbols? (c) Is this key a good choice for this data? Explain briefly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Street 1: 3 symbols; Street 2: 5 symbols; Street 3: 2 symbols; Street 4: 4 symbols; Street 5: 3 full + 1 half symbol (3.5 symbols). (b) Street 2 requires the most symbols (5). (c) The key is a reasonable choice: most values divide evenly by 10, and the maximum number of symbols (5) is manageable. Street 5's value of 35 requires a half-symbol, which is acceptable but does introduce a minor complication — the student might note that a key of 1 symbol = 5 bicycles would avoid half-symbols entirely, at the cost of more symbols per row.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each street's bicycle count by the key value (10) to find the number of symbols, using a half-symbol for a remainder of 5.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line from 0 to 50 in steps of 10 and mark each street's value to see how many full groups of 10 fit.
inclusivity.challenge: Choose a different key (e.g., 1 symbol = 5 bicycles) and redo part (a) — does the new key avoid half-symbols? What trade-off does it introduce?

items.prompt: A horizontal bar graph shows the number of books sold by a stall on five days of a fair. The scale is 1 unit = 20 books. The bar lengths (in units on the scale) are: Monday 4, Tuesday 7, Wednesday 5, Thursday 9, Friday 6. (a) How many books were sold on Tuesday? (b) On which day were the most books sold? (c) How many total books were sold across all five days? (d) How many more books were sold on Thursday than on Monday?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Tuesday: 7 × 20 = 140 books. (b) Thursday had the highest bar (9 units), so the most books were sold on Thursday. (c) Total units = 4 + 7 + 5 + 9 + 6 = 31 units; total books = 31 × 20 = 620 books. (d) Thursday − Monday = (9 − 4) × 20 = 5 × 20 = 100 more books.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each bar's unit-length by the scale factor (20) to convert to books, then add, compare, or subtract as required.

inclusivity.support: Draw a simple number line from 0 to 9 and mark each bar length, then multiply each by 20 using a multiplication table.
inclusivity.challenge: If the scale were changed to 1 unit = 50 books, what bar lengths would Thursday and Monday have? Re-draw those two bars.

items.prompt: A student records the number of birds spotted in a park over six mornings: Sparrows 40, Pigeons 60, Crows 80, Mynas 50, Parrots 20, Bulbuls 30. She wants to draw a vertical bar graph. (a) What scale would you recommend (1 unit = ? birds) so that the tallest bar needs no more than 8 units? Show your reasoning. (b) Using your chosen scale, what is the bar height in units for Crows? (c) What is the bar height in units for Parrots?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) The maximum value is 80 birds. We need 80 ÷ scale ≤ 8, so scale ≥ 10. A scale of 1 unit = 10 birds gives a maximum bar height of 8 units — exactly 8, which is acceptable. (b) Crows: 80 ÷ 10 = 8 units. (c) Parrots: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the maximum data value by the desired maximum bar height to determine the minimum scale unit, then confirm all values divide evenly.

inclusivity.support: List the six values and try dividing each by 10 first — if all give whole numbers, 1 unit = 10 is a good scale.
inclusivity.challenge: The student adds a seventh morning: Kingfishers 25. Does your scale still work without introducing fractional bar heights? If not, what new scale would you choose?

items.prompt: Ravi records the number of customers who visit a small shop each day: Monday 35, Tuesday 50, Wednesday 45, Thursday 60, Friday 55, Saturday 70. He draws a vertical bar graph using a scale of 1 unit = 5 customers. (a) What is the bar height in units for Saturday? (b) What is the bar height in units for Monday? (c) What is the difference in bar height (in units) between the busiest day and the least busy day?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Saturday: 70 ÷ 5 = 14 units. (b) Monday: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 units. (c) Busiest day = Saturday (70, 14 units); least busy = Monday (35, 7 units); difference = 14 − 7 = 7 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each frequency by the scale unit (5) to compute bar heights, then subtract the smallest from the largest to find the difference in units.

inclusivity.support: Use a multiplication table for 5 to find how many 5s fit into each customer count before drawing the bar.
inclusivity.challenge: If Ravi adds a Sunday with 25 customers, how does the bar graph change? What is the new difference between the tallest and shortest bars?

items.prompt: A student rolls a die 20 times and records the outcomes in a frequency table: 1 appears 4 times, 2 appears 2 times, 3 appears 5 times, 4 appears 3 times, 5 appears 1 time, 6 appears 5 times. (a) Which number appeared the maximum number of times? (b) Which number appeared the minimum number of times? (c) What is the total count of all outcomes? Does this match the number of rolls? (d) Two numbers appeared the same number of times — which are they?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) 3 and 6 both appeared the maximum number of times (5 times each). (b) 5 appeared the minimum number of times (1 time). (c) Total = 4 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 1 + 5 = 20, which matches the 20 rolls. (d) The numbers that appeared the same number of times are 3 and 6 (each 5 times).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the frequency column to identify the maximum, minimum, sum (total), and any equal values.

inclusivity.support: Circle the largest number in the frequency column, then the smallest, and add all six frequencies one by one to find the total.
inclusivity.challenge: If the student rolls the die 10 more times and each of the six outcomes appears once more in those rolls, update the frequency table and re-answer all four parts.
